title: Fatal outcome of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) in a lupus nephropathy patient: A case report
case_prompt:
A 14-year-old girl with a history of biopsy-proven lupus nephropathy maintained on mycophenolic acid (500 mg/day) and prednisolone (40 mg/day) presented with a 3-day history of headache and her first generalized seizure. She had also received two doses of an mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 12/15. Her blood pressure was 190/117 mm Hg, heart rate 150 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She had generalized edema and a urinary tract infection but no meningeal signs. Metabolic causes were eliminated.

Laboratory studies revealed:
  • Creatinine 18.47 mg/L  
  • Potassium 5.6 mmol/L  
  • ESR 116 mm/h  
  • Hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL  
  • WBC count 28.12 × 10^3/mm^3  
  • CRP 58 mg/L  
  • Procalcitonin 5.9 ng/mL  
  • ANA positive  

A noncontrast CT scan of the brain demonstrated subtle bilateral, grossly symmetrical cortical and subcortical hypodensities in the posterior parietal lobes, which remained unchanged after contrast administration.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. PRES is suggested by characteristically symmetric posterior hypodensities on CT—“Axial CT obtained day 1 of admission, showing subtle bilateral, grossly symmetrical, cortical and sub-cortical posterior parietal hypodensities…consistent with PRES.”  
2. Lupus cerebritis and neuropsychiatric lupus were considered given her SLED history—“Differential diagnosis for PRES in a patient with a pre-established diagnosis of SLED, includes lupus cerebritis, neuropsychiatric-lupus…”  
3. Meningitis was contemplated but is unlikely in the absence of meningeal signs and typical CSF findings—“she had no meningeal signs…and metabolic causes were eliminated” and “A lumbar puncture could be useful to eliminate meningitis…However, cerebrospinal fluid in PRES often only shows moderately elevated protein levels with less than 5 leucocytes/µl.”  
4. Ischemic stroke was excluded by diffusion imaging characteristics—“Diffusion-weighted imaging is mainly useful to differentiate PRES from ischemia, as we find low intensity signal lesions in PRES…high intensity signal lesions in cerebral ischemia…”  
5. Intracranial hemorrhage was ruled out on CT by the absence of hyperdense lesions or enhancement—“Axial CT…unchanged before (A) and after contrast (B), consistent with PRES.”  
6. A primary seizure disorder was less likely given the new severe hypertension and imaging abnormalities—“Differential diagnosis for PRES…includes…a primary seizure disorder and many others, and PRES should be considered an elimination diagnosis with supportive findings.”
